blocks.text: On the night of 19th of Feb, 1950, across whole of Punjab, the British take the keys to every arms depot out of Indian hands. Every Indian sentry is replaced by a European. In one night, the Raj has sensed a mutiny inside its own army, the kind it has not seen since 1857. And the man it was most afraid of that night is 19 years old. The mutiny did not start in India. It started 7,000 miles away in the lumber bunkhouses of Pacific Northwest. And it brought the British Empire within  days of total military collapse. This is the

story of how they almost pulled it off and why, a century later, it is a history most Indians were never taught. To understand why Punjabi men are in California, you need to understand the Punjab they left. Six famines have hit Punjab since British rule begin. Six million dead. And the Raj's taxation has made farming unviable for the men who survived them. So, they leave. They lay railway lines. They cut timber in the logging camps of North American West

Coast. They work long hours and sleep eight to 10 in a log cabin. By 1910, about 10,000 Indians are on Pacific Coast. If you do better than that, Jawala Singh grows potatoes in Sacramento Delta. Enough of them that people call him Potato King. Remember him. His money is going to fund a revolution. And the scholarship he sets up in Guru Gobind Singh's name is going to bring bright young Indians to universities across California. Almost every one of them ends up in the network

aimed at British Raj from American soil. Most of the Sikhs prefer Canada. They are the subject of British Empire and Canada is in the Empire. Then the Canadian government wakes up to a growing non-white population. >> Whites, >>  >> Canada  forever. Whites, Canada forever. >> And passes laws to stop immigration from Asia. Think about who those laws hit, ex-soldiers of British Raj, men who fought empires colonial wars, told at the empire's door that they are not

wanted. Two educated revolutionaries arrive from India and give that anger a shape. Taraknath Das from Anushilan Samiti organizes protest against the racist laws and prints periodical Free Hindustan. Harnam Singh, a former Sikh soldier, does the same in Punjabi in Gurmukhi script. Every month, they organize through gurdwaras of Vancouver for civil rights at first. British intelligence in India is alarmed enough to send a man. William Hopkinson, born in India, fluent in Punjabi and Hindi.

His job is to get inside the gurdwara networks and replace the patriots with loyalist. Keep his name. He's going to be in the story until the end of it. His first target is Taraknath Das, who has been telling Sikh soldiers to raise. Canada expels him. He goes south and  keeps printing. By 1911, the hostility is bad enough that Indians start leaving Canada altogether, moving down the coast to United States, to California. >> Since then, people have been coming to California in search of many things.

Cabrillo was the first in 1542. >>  >> And he sought new lands and treasure. More than two centuries later in 1769,  came the first colonizers, the Spanish padres, seeking through their chain of missions to establish a new outpost of Christianity in a heathen world. >> They are leaving a country the British rule for the one that threw the British out, but the racism does not end. After Swami Vivekananda, American elite from Boston to San Francisco are exploring

Hindu philosophy. American politicians and religious leaders feel threatened by it. In segregated America, Indians are kept out of the hotels, trains, and the theaters. They are called the scum of the Orient. 500 white men riot against Indian immigrants, but the America gives the revolutionaries the one thing Canada could not, distance from the British Isles. In 1911, member of Savarkar's Abhinav Bharat, Lala Hardayal, arrives in San Francisco. He settles near University of California and becomes so

popular that Stanford University invites him to deliver lectures in Hindu philosophy and Sanskrit. By 1912, his network reached past the students and into the mills because a Namdhari Sikh named Sohan Singh Bhakna  has been building it among Punjabi workers in Portland. In March 1913, Hardayal comes to Portland to speak. The students and the mill workers join hand with one aim, the British out of India. They found the Pacific Coast Hindustan Association. Jwala Singh and

other working-class Punjabis generously contributed for the funding. Then they gave it a structure, and this is the part worth noticing. Eight towns on the West Coast, each elected two men to a central committee with two-year terms, a meeting every three months. They have two jobs, teach politics and collect money. Elected officers and a treasury, nobody has built this for India before, anywhere in the world. Their newspaper is called Ghadar. The word means mutiny. It is printed in hand, in Urdu and in Punjabi. Its editor is 17. He is one of

the students. Kartar Singh Sarabha has come to America to study at University of California. He drops out of the university, moves in with Hardayal as his assistant and runs the paper. Published in foreign land, yet written in the language of India, it announced the beginning of a war against the British rule. It then laid out the plan in explicit terms, turn Indian soldiers against the British officers, release prisoners from the jails, seize the government treasuries, and sever the railway and telegraph networks. There was no attempt to conceal the program.

It appeared openly on the front page and was then circulated across India through the post. Remember his name, too. A boy in Punjab is going to grow up on it. Most of the men the paper is for cannot read it. So, the students read it out to them loudly in the fields and the camps until men who could not read a word know the paper anyway. It goes by post  and by hand to Singapore, Manila, Trinidad through the gurdwaras. And the gurdwaras do better than deliver it. They sing it. Its words are sung at worship. A paper in Gurmukhi reaches men

who cannot read Gurmukhi. Hopkinson's people are inside those gurdwaras now, and the alarm goes to India. The Raj bans the paper.  In January 1914, the port at Bombay seizes 215 bundles of it, and then a ship does more for the movement than newspaper ever did. Canada has been sealing its door, and Punjabis are stranded across East Asia. Many of them are relatives of men already in British Columbia. A court gives them a hopeful verdict. So, in 1914, a businessman named Gurdit Singh

charters a Japanese cooling ship, Komagata Maru, retrofitted to carry humans. It leaves Hong Kong in April with 366 people aboard. Many of them read Ghadar. Almost none of them are in the movement. They were passengers, at least for now. They reach Vancouver in May. They are not allowed off the ship, so they stay on it at the anchor with the city in sight. For 2 months,  350 men live on coal ship. Water is rationed, food runs short, and at  times the officials on shore hold the supplies back to make the point. The summer heat sits on the

steel. There is no privacy  and nowhere to wash. Men fell sick, and every morning they can see the shore, and the people on the shore can see them, and some of the men standing on the docks are their relatives. The story is widely reported, and it  angers the Indian community up and down the northwest coast. Hopkinson plays a crucial role in actively blocking the Indian Shore Committee and legal  counsel from helping the passengers. On the shore, he runs an extensive network of paid informants inside the Gurudwaras to sabotage the relief efforts. The Sikh

community raises $20,000 and takes the case to the court. They lose. In July, the ship is escorted out of harbor by Royal Navy cruiser. At Yokohama, Sohan Singh Bhakna comes aboard and talks to them. By now, he has a very willing audience. He also puts pistols on the ship. Hopkinson advises that nobody be let off before Calcutta. So, in Shanghai, Hong Kong, and Singapore, nobody is. And in every port, Indians watch. In September, the ship anchors at Budge Budge near Calcutta, 6 months

after it sailed. 6 months on a coal ship. The British government suspects them of being revolutionaries. The plan is to put them straight onto train for Punjab. Gurdit Singh lifts the Guru Granth Sahib and walks to the local Gurudwara instead.  Most of them walk behind him. It is dark. The police were everywhere and the shooting starts. 18 passengers are killed. More than 200 arrested. In North America, Ghadarites start killing men suspected of spying for the British. A Ghadar activist named Mewa Singh walks into a local courthouse

and shoots Hopkinson dead. The British Empire's treatment of ship's passenger becomes the movement's  best recruiting tool. And the newspapers started openly calling for rebellion. British intelligence suspects what was coming  and starts arresting Sikhs returning from North America. And then, Europe goes to war. >> August 1914. Across Europe,  men have been called up to fight. The number is already unprecedented in military history. >>

>> The empire is distracted and stretched thin. Britain's weakness has always been India's opportunity. Now, that opportunity has arrived. In Varanasi, Sachindra Nath Sanyal and Rash Behari Bose are working on the same thing from the other side, an uprising  inside the British Army in India. Bose has already tried to kill Viceroy with a bomb. His network in Punjab is in touch  with Ghadarites coming home. They come long way to escape British eyes. Some smuggled across the frontier with German

officials helping. Why Germans? Because Germany wants the uprising, too. British work out what was coming, and they do something revealing. They give an order to shipping lines.  Indians passing through can no longer step ashore at Singapore, Hong Kong, or Penang.  Why those three? Each one of those has Indian regiments garrisoned in it. The Potato King, Jawala Singh, sails for  India with $50,000 for funding the uprising. It was taken off him the day he lands, and he was arrested. Kartar Singh and Vishnu Ganesh Pingale are already inside India. Bhagga Jatin introduces them to

Bose  and Sanyal. Sanyal needs a man he can trust in Lahore and Amritsar, so Kartar Singh takes it. Pingale goes  to barracks at Meerut. Bhagga Jatin will raise the Bengal. Sanyal faces in Varanasi to coordinate  the United Provinces. So, what is the largest political organization in India doing in these same weeks? Since Bal Gangadhar Tilak's arrest, moderates have run the Congress. They met at Madras that December. Resolution five thanks the Viceroy for sending >>  >> Indian troops to the war. Resolution 19

records the Congress's pride in those troops. Seven weeks later, the Ghadarites will try to make those same troops mutiny, because that was always the target. The soldiers holding India down are Indians. The whole plan rests on changing whose side they are on. The weapons are supposed to come from Germany. 8,000 rifles, 4 million rounds, go to San Diego to be moved at sea from a ship to a tanker. The tanker never  comes. By their own account, no more than 200 pistols cross the Pacific in six months. They set the date, anyway, 21st of Feb, 1915. It starts at

Mian Mir Cantonment in Lahore, and that is the signal for everywhere else. And by then, there is a man inside the room reporting to the police. On 13th Feb, one of their men is arrested. Two days later, another one, Kirpal Singh, is seen talking to police officer at Lahore station. Kirpal sits in the inner circle. They know something has gone wrong, so they move the raising forward to 19th. He reports  that too. Hours before the signal, the police raid the houses in Lahore. Within no time, across the province,  in one night, every Indian guard at arms depot

is replaced by a European. Kartar Singh goes to Ferozepur that evening anyway. >>  >> The soldiers he has come to raise are already disarmed. The only place the mutiny actually happens that Feb is Singapore, one of the three ports the British sealed. The regiments there are mostly Muslims, and they have heard they may be sent to fight the Ottoman Sultan. To crush the revolutionary network, the British rush through the Defense of India Act. It completely throws out ordinary criminal law. Three

government-appointed commissioners can sentence a man to hang with zero right to appeal. There is an outcry across the country, yet the elected Indian members on Imperial Legislative Council pass it unanimously. The council accepts just two minor amendments, and the Viceroy notes in private that he granted them merely to save their faces. The historian documenting this is R.C. Majumdar. He calls it the eternal disgrace of the moderate school of politics in India. Nine mass trials took place throughout 1915. 291 men are

convicted. A lot of Ghadarites were arrested at port towns. 42 are sent to gallows. The manhunt is actively assisted by Punjabi elites, including the chief of Khalsa Diwan. Rashbehari Bose escapes to Japan. Sachindra Nath Sanyal is arrested, but narrowly escapes the rope. At his trial, the British judge calls Kartar Singh the most dangerous man in the dock. Kartar Singh replies, "I shall prefer death so that I can be reborn till Hindustan is liberated and go to gallows again and again. He is hanged alongside Pingley at

Lahore Central Jail on 16th of November, 1915. He was 19. He becomes an inspiration for another revolutionary, Bhagat Singh. >> Although this whole episode had failed >>  >> in carrying out a 1857 type insurrection, these ideas of the Ghadarites, however, remained alive.  And when the Indian soldiers began to return after the First World War in 1919, the British were very, very concerned that this would lead to a big

revolt because you now had all these well-trained, armed, and organized groups returning and increasingly radicalized by these ideas. This is the context in which they introduced the Rowlatt Act and  the draconian Rowlatt Act ultimately led to the succession of events that led to the Jallianwala Bagh  massacre. So, >> the Ghadar Party never fired a grand shot it had prepared. What it built instead was the first modern Indian revolutionary network abroad. Its

operations were spanning across four continents, aimed directly at the single pillar the British rule could not survive without.  So, why is the movement of this scale not the story most Indians are told?
